segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The virgins played with passion by Lillian Gish and with humor by Mary Pickford during the silent era were countered by two comparatively short-lived manifestations of the sexualized woman. In the mid-1910s came the vamp, the voracious upper-class man-eater, iconically portrayed by Theda Bara in A Fool There Was (1915). In the 1920s, the vamp gave way to the flapper, a hedonistic but not at all malicious figure, most successfully embodied by Colleen Moore and Clara Bow, the It Girl.

In the nineteen twenties, the vamp gave way to the flapper, a hedonistic but not at all malicious figure, most successfully embodied by Colleen Moore and Clara Bow, the It Girl.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Virgins and vamps hark back to Victorian melodrama and were fantasies rooted in idealized and demonized notions of femininity. Having arrived after World War I, the flapper was one facet of the new emancipated woman, who worked, voted, smoked, drank, danced to jazz and had sex. The other facet was the sophisticated wife, played with great daring by Gloria Swanson (1899-1983) and her extravagant outfits in six bedroom comedies by Cecil B. DeMille (1881-1959). The sexy working girl and the liberated wife merged into one, giving rise to the sharp-tongued modern woman of the screwball comedy, or madcap comedy, of the 1930s, a subgenre that can be considered the forerunner of the romantic comedy.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Just as the femme fatale of 1940s film noir was a product of male anxieties during a period of national instability, the vamp was a sociological construct. Unlike the femme fatale, however, she would not later be redeemed by feminist scholars. She emerged as a celluloid phantom, drawn from Sir Philip Burne-Jones's painting The Vampire, from the poem of the same name by his cousin Rudyard Kipling and from the novel Dracula by Bram Stoker, all from 1897. Kipling's poem inspired the Broadway play A Fool There Was, a 1909 hit directed by Porter Emerson Browne and adapted for the screen in 1915.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Bara explored her vampish traits in a series of seductive characters, her eyes painted black, most recognizably in Cleopatra (1917). However, Bara was not American cinema's first vampire. Alice Hollister preceded her in The Vampire (1913), in which vaudeville dancers Alice Eis and Bert French re-created their "Vampire Dance," which had been a stage hit in 1909. As a supernatural woman who sucks the life force out of a lawyer, Bara became the most sensual of all the femme fatales.

segments.original: Theda Bara was neither the first nor the last star to have her name changed by the Hollywood studios. Florence Lawrence, "The Biograph Girl," considered the "first movie star," who in 1910 also became the first actress to have her real name in the credits, was actually Florence Annie Bridgwood.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Many other stars were given — or chose, though this was rarer — stage names. Sometimes it was a matter of euphony: Julius Ulman became Douglas Fairbanks, while Frances Gumm metamorphosed into Judy Garland. Some names carried unfortunate associations: Hedwig Kiesler's surname was considered too similar to keister (slang for "rear end"), and so she became Hedy Lamarr.

segments.original: Alice Guy Blaché had been hired as a secretary at the Comptoir Général de Photographie, which would be acquired the following year by Léon Gaumont. Under the Gaumont name, the world's first film company was born — and the oldest still in operation. Despite the change at the company, the young woman, then in her twenties, kept working as a secretary — but she would not stay in the job for long.

tracks.title: La Sortie de l’usine Lumière à Lyon

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Together with the Gaumont team, Alice Guy was invited to witness the magic of the first cinematograph developed by the Lumière brothers. The device, revolutionary for its time, worked as both camera and projector. As she watched the scenes of La Sortie de l’usine Lumière à Lyon (Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory, 1895), she foresaw the potential of the new technology. The daughter of a bookseller, Alice had always been used to reading and had even done some theater for a while. Her familiarity with storytelling led her to look at cinema in a new way. She decided to turn it into a vehicle for telling stories.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Although the Lumière brothers made a short scene titled L’Arroseur arrosé (The Sprinkler Sprinkled, 1895) in 1895, they had no inkling of cinema's full potential and saw it more as a tool for recording than as a way of telling stories. In contrast, Alice Guy's first film features sets, cuts, special effects and a narrative, however brief. It is based on an old French legend according to which baby boys are born from cabbages, while girls are born from roses.

segments.original: According to her granddaughter Adrienne Blaché-Channing in The Lost Garden: The Life and Cinema of Alice Guy-Blaché (1995), Alice's first commercial film sold 80 copies, a success for its time. Its strong reception led the young woman to be quickly promoted to head of film production at Gaumont. Quite a position for a woman in the 19th century.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The greatest success of her career came the same year, when Alice released La Vie du Christ (The Birth, the Life and the Death of Christ, 1906), a 34-minute short film that explores film language as never before. With special effects, scene cuts and deep characters, she laid the first foundation upon which the blockbusters of the future would be built. Also in 1906, the director released the film Les résultats du féminisme (The Consequences of Feminism, 1906), which shows men performing activities typically associated with women, while the women enjoy themselves at the bar and harass their partners. In less than 7 minutes, the comedy uses laughter to poke at the status quo.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: On a business trip, the director met her colleague Herbert Blaché, whom she married, and was removed from her post at Gaumont – he, of course, kept his job. In 1907, her husband was sent to the United States as the company's production manager. Determined to start a new life in America, they packed their bags. Once in the United States, Alice founded her own company, Solax, in 1910. The first productions were a success, and by 1912 she was the only woman in the country earning more than $25,000 a year. With that success, she built her own studio in Fort Lee for $100,000 – the equivalent of a $3 million investment today.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The director is believed to have worked on more than a thousand film productions, although only 130 of them have been found to date. Over time, many of her films were credited to men, while others bore only the name of the production company. Her work began to be rediscovered in the '80s, after the posthumous publication of her autobiography, written in the late '40s. In the book, Alice lists the films she produced, in the hope of one day receiving due credit for her work and claiming a place that had always been hers: that of a pioneer of cinema.
